subChunks.title: Math & Random

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin leads you to the Great Mathematical Grimoire — a vast tome bound in bronze, its pages shimmering with pre-written incantations.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every wizard who ever lived has needed to take a square root, find the larger of two numbers, or roll a magical die. Do not waste your arcane energy writing these from scratch. The Grimoire — Java's Math class — contains them all.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And for randomness — every great ritual needs an element of the unknown. The Random class is your magical die. Give it a seed and the sequence becomes perfectly repeatable — essential for testing your spells reliably.

storyBeats.label: Rolling the magical die

guidedPractice.problemHtml:
Print the following, each on its own line:

  1. Math.pow(2, 10) — should print 1024.0
  2. Math.sqrt(144.0) — should print 12.0
  3. Math.round(3.7) — should print 4
  4. The string Rolling dice...
guidedPractice.hint: All Math methods are static — call them directly as Math.pow(), Math.sqrt(), etc.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Name five Math class methods and explain what each one does, including its parameter types and return type.

questions.explanation: Math.round rounds to the nearest integer. When the fractional part is exactly 0.5, Java rounds up (towards positive infinity), so 3.5 becomes 4. The return type for a double argument is long.

questions.prompt:
What does this code print? 
System.out.println(Math.max(15, Math.min(20, 10)));
How do you generate a random integer between 1 and 10 inclusive using Random?
questions.explanation: nextInt(10) returns 0–9. Adding 1 shifts the range to 1–10. nextInt(11) gives 0–10. nextInt(1, 10) is a newer overload but gives 1–9, not 1–10.
Math.floor always returns a double. Math.floor(3.9) returns 3.0, not 3. If you need an int, you must cast: (int) Math.floor(3.9).

subChunks.title: Date & Time (java.time)

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin enchants a glowing calendar on the wall of his study. Dates ripple and shift as he gestures.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The old Calendar grimoire was a disaster — months started at zero, nothing was immutable, and time zones were a nightmare. In Java 8, we rewrote the entire chapter. Meet java.time: clean, immutable, and sensible.

storyBeats.label: A magical contract date

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice: calling plusDays does not change signed. It creates a brand new date object. All java.time objects are immutable — a deliberate design choice that prevents many subtle bugs.
The calendar pulses softly, the contract date highlighted in gold — exactly thirty days after signing, to the second.

guidedPractice.problemHtml:
Perform the following operations:

  1. Create a LocalDate for 2025-01-15 using LocalDate.of().
  2. Add 30 days to get the expiry date.
  3. Print the expiry date (default format is yyyy-MM-dd).

Expected output: 2025-02-14
guidedPractice.hint: LocalDate.of(year, month, day) — months are 1-indexed (not 0-indexed like the old Calendar API).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the java.time package. Why was it introduced in Java 8? What are the key differences from java.util.Date?

questions.prompt: Which class would you use to represent a date without a time or timezone?
questions.explanation: LocalDate holds only a year, month, and day — no time, no timezone. LocalDateTime adds time; ZonedDateTime adds a timezone.

questions.prompt: Calling plusDays(10) on a LocalDate modifies the original object.
questions.explanation: All java.time objects are immutable. plusDays returns a new LocalDate object; the original is unchanged. You must capture the return value.
2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days. plusDays(1) from Feb 28 gives Feb 29. LocalDate.toString() uses ISO format: yyyy-MM-dd.

questions.prompt: You need to calculate the number of days between two LocalDate values. Which class do you use?
questions.explanation: Period represents a date-based amount (years, months, days) and is used with LocalDate. Duration is for time-based amounts (nanoseconds to hours) and works with LocalTime or Instant.

subChunks.title: Enums

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin stands before four crystalline orbs, each radiating a different energy.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The four schools of magic: FIRE, WATER, EARTH, AIR. These are not arbitrary strings. They are a fixed, known set. No apprentice can invent a fifth school by typo. This is what an enum gives you — a closed, type-safe catalogue.

storyBeats.label: The four schools

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice how cleanly this reads in a switch statement. And because the compiler knows all possible values, it can warn you if you forget to handle one in a switch expression. Try representing that with integers.

One of the apprentices raises a hand. "Can an enum have methods?" Eldrin smiles. "An enum is a full class. It can have fields, constructors, and methods. But today, keep it simple — master the basics first."

guidedPractice.problemHtml:
Define a Season enum with values SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN, WINTER. Write a method getDescription(Season s) that returns a short phrase for each season using a switch statement. In main, print the descriptions for SUMMER and WINTER.

Expected output:

Warm and sunny
Cold and dark
guidedPractice.hint: Each case in the switch should return a String. Use System.out.println(getDescription(Season.SUMMER)) etc.

tests.label: Season descriptions
tests.expected:
Warm and sunny
Cold and dark

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is an enum in Java? How is it different from using int constants or String constants for a fixed set of values?

questions.prompt: What does Season.WINTER.ordinal() return if the enum is declared as SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN, WINTER?
questions.explanation: ordinal() returns the zero-based position of the constant in the enum declaration. SPRING=0, SUMMER=1, AUTUMN=2, WINTER=3.
name() returns the constant's name as a String: "GREEN". ordinal() returns its zero-based position: RED=0, GREEN=1, BLUE=2.

questions.prompt: An enum in Java can have fields and methods.
questions.explanation: Enums are full class types in Java. You can add fields, constructors, and methods. Each constant can also override methods individually, making enums very powerful beyond simple constants.

questions.prompt: Why is using an enum better than using int constants for a fixed set of values?
options: Enums are type-safe — the compiler rejects invalid values; int constants allow any integer
Enums are faster at runtime than ints
Enums can only hold four values
Int constants cannot be used in switch statements
questions.answer: Enums are type-safe — the compiler rejects invalid values; int constants allow any integer
questions.explanation: With int constants, nothing stops a caller from passing 99 as a 'direction'. Enums constrain the type to only the declared values, catching mistakes at compile time. They also provide built-in name(), ordinal(), and meaningful toString().

subChunks.title: Optional & Varargs

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin opens the Academy's spell catalogue — a book where some entries exist and some do not.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When a student looks up a spell that doesn't exist, the old system returned null. Null is a lie — it means 'nothing', but the type says 'a thing'. Optional tells the truth: 'this method might return a Spell, or it might not.' The absence is part of the contract.

storyBeats.label: Spell lookup with Optional

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And varargs — some spells accept one ingredient, some accept ten. You don't write ten overloaded methods. You write one method with String... ingredients and let the caller pass as many as needed.

storyBeats.label: Varargs ingredient list

guidedPractice.problemHtml:
Part 1 — Optional: Write findSpell(String name) that returns Optional.of(name) if name.equals("Fireball"), otherwise Optional.empty(). Print results using orElse("Spell not found").

Part 2 — Varargs: Write sum(int... numbers) that totals all arguments. Print sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).

Expected output (three lines):

Fireball
Spell not found
15
guidedPractice.hint: Internally, int... numbers is treated as an int[] — you can loop over it with a for-each.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What problem does Optional solve in Java? How is it better than returning null from a method?

questions.explanation: Optional.ofNullable(null) creates an empty Optional. orElse("default") returns the fallback value when the Optional is empty.
The varargs method iterates over the three arguments: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

questions.prompt: Varargs parameters must be the last parameter in a method's parameter list.
questions.explanation: Java requires varargs (type... name) to be the final parameter. This is because the compiler converts it to an array, and there can be only one such variable-length parameter per method.

questions.prompt: You have an Optional<String> opt that may or may not hold a value. Which approach is safest?
questions.explanation: opt.get() throws NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty. orElse safely returns a fallback. An Optional is never null itself (it's either present or empty), so null-checking the Optional is wrong.
